points.title: Why hex matches binary
points.must: 16 = 2⁴, so one hex digit represents exactly 4 bits (one nibble).

points.title: Hex digit table
points.must: The table of hex digits 0–F with their denary values and 4-bit binary patterns.

points.title: Binary → hex
points.must: Split into nibbles from the right, pad with leading 0s, convert each nibble (e.g. 11010011 = D3; 101101 = 2D).

points.title: Hex → binary
points.must: Each hex digit becomes exactly 4 bits (e.g. 5C = 0101 1100).

points.title: Hex → denary
points.must: Multiply each digit by its place value 256, 16, 1 and add (7A = 122; 1F4 = 500).

points.title: Denary → hex
points.must: Divide by 16: quotient then remainder, or go via binary (245 = F5).

points.title: Worked example
points.must: A conversion in a real context, e.g. printer error code 3C = 60 = 00111100.

points.title: Hex is only for people
points.must: The computer stores and processes binary; hex is a shorthand to display binary for humans.

points.title: Advantages of hexadecimal
points.must: Shorter (2 digits per byte), easier to read/remember, fewer copying errors, easy conversion to binary, lines up with bytes — each with a reason.

points.title: Uses of hexadecimal
points.must: At least four: colour codes, MAC addresses, memory addresses / machine code, error codes, IPv6, Unicode.

points.title: Colour code example
points.must: #2E8B57 split into three bytes: red 46, green 139, blue 87; 3 bytes = 24 bits.

points.title: MAC address example
points.must: 6 bytes = 48 bits = 12 hex digits; easier to read than 48 binary digits.

points.title: Hex vs denary
points.must: Hex lines up with nibbles and converts digit by digit; denary needs arithmetic and does not line up.

points.title: Prefixes
points.must: 0x, #, h or subscript 16 show that a number is hexadecimal.
